The Metternich Stela records Thoth declaring that he has come from the sky by command of the Sun. He says that he has come to make protection at the bed, both day and night, and extends this protection to any suffering person. Isis then reassures Horus, telling him not to fear and promising that she will be around him as protection.

Within the text's own terms, protection comes through divine presence and speech. Thoth stands watch under the Sun's command, while Isis surrounds the vulnerable person. The recitation gives these divine declarations a place beside the bed and applies the promise not only to Horus but also to any sufferer.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this passage can be approached as a study of how reassurance, divine authority, and bedside language were joined in an Egyptian protective text. It remains uncertain how often this specific recitation was used at a bedside or how its effects were understood in practice. Its surviving wording nevertheless makes care and protection the central themes.
reflection: What might change in the meaning of this recitation when its promise of protection is extended from Horus to any person who is suffering?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the two recorded passages aloud once, identifying when the speaker is Thoth and when the speaker is Isis. Then write one sentence about how each voice expresses protection.
sourceCitation: Metternich Stela (Metropolitan Museum of Art 50.85) - Metternich Stela, section A

title: To Be Said on Water or on Land
intro: This lesson examines a protective invocation from the Metternich Stela, a 30th Dynasty text from the 4th century BC. The passage is explicitly presented as valid on water or on land.
body:
The Metternich Stela, held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art as 50.85, records this passage in section H, identified as Thoth's invocation of Horus. It gives a general protective appeal and asks Horus to bar lions at the desert edge, crocodiles on the river, and every biting mouth in its cavern. It closes with the words, "I am Horus the Saviour."

In the text's own terms, Thoth's declaration establishes the force of the recitation: "I have recited with your magic, I have spoken with your effectiveness, I have enchanted with your words." The spoken formula is joined to Horus's protective authority, sealing the mouths of crawling things in sky, earth, and water.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this passage can be approached as a study of how spoken authority and divine identity were joined to protection across different environments. It remains uncertain how this specific passage was performed in daily life or how broadly its users understood the protection to extend. The record presents a historical reconstruction for study and reading, not a modern prescription.
reflection: What changes when a protective formula is imagined as working equally on water and on land, against dangers associated with each environment?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, read the recorded declaration and closing sentence slowly, then write a few lines about the kinds of danger or vulnerability the passage names. Keep the exercise focused on historical reflection rather than attempting to control animals or other people.
safetyNote: The historical passage refers to lions, crocodiles, and other biting creatures. Study it from a safe distance and do not approach, handle, or attempt to control wildlife.
sourceCitation: Metternich Stela (Metropolitan Museum of Art 50.85) - Metternich Stela, section H, Thoth's invocation of Horus

title: You Are My Reflection
intro: This lesson presents the closing act recorded at the end of Maqlu VIII. It centers on looking into water in morning light and affirming ownership of one's reflection and identity.
body:
Maqlu records this act as the closing of the working. In the morning, the patient looks into a clean bowl filled with pure water while morning light falls on it. The recorded words address the reflection directly: "You are my reflection... You are mine, and I am yours. May nobody know you, may no evil approach you!" The working ends there.

In its own terms, the act treats the reflection as something connected to the patient's identity. Claiming it as both "mine" and "yours" restores that connection after witchcraft had loosened it. The wish that nobody know it and that no evil approach it gives the closing a protective purpose.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this can be understood as a focused act of recognition: a person uses a visible reflection and spoken words to mark a return to a sense of self. The record does not explain exactly how the loosening of identity was understood or experienced, and that remains uncertain. Its final instruction is simple: after the words are spoken, the working ends.
reflection: What might it mean to claim your own reflection as a way of marking the return of a sense of identity?
practice: As a modern reflective practice, look at your reflection in a mirror or a bowl of water and write one sentence about what feels recognizably yours today. This is a present-day exercise in attention, not a reconstruction of the historical rite.
sourceCitation: Maqlu VIII, 127-137

title: You Who Are in the Hole
intro: This lesson studies a protective address against a hidden creature that might bite, sting, or release poison. It comes from the Metternich Stela, section G, identified as Thoth's spell for Horus.
body:
The Metternich Stela records this spell in the 30th Dynasty, in the 4th century BC. The source is held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art, with the citation identifying section G as Thoth's spell for Horus. The address begins by naming the creature as one in a hole or on a path.

The spell identifies the sufferer with the Sun, Thoth, Nefertem, and the son of Osiris. It then forbids the hidden creature to bite, sting, or shoot poison at him. The command You shall spew out is repeated four times, making expulsion the final force of the address.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this text shows a logic in which protection is created through direct speech and identification with powerful sacred figures. The repeated command gives the lesson a strong rhythm while describing the removal of poison. It remains uncertain how this text was performed in every historical setting or what results people believed it produced. This entry is a historical reconstruction for study and reading, not a modern prescription.
reflection: What does the spell's identification of the sufferer with the Sun, Thoth, Nefertem, and the son of Osiris suggest about how protection was imagined in this text?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, read the recorded address quietly and journal about how its repeated command changes your sense of urgency or protection. Do not treat the reading as protection from an actual bite, sting, or poison.
safetyNote: The historical material concerns bites, stings, and poison and is recorded for study. Do not rely on this spell as medical treatment; seek appropriate medical help after an actual bite or sting.
sourceCitation: Metternich Stela (Metropolitan Museum of Art 50.85) - Metternich Stela, section G, Thoth's spell for Horus

title: Your Mouth Has Been Shut by the Sun
intro: This lesson studies a four-part protective formula from the Ancient Egyptian Metternich Stela. It is described as a spell for protection on water and ends by extending protection to people and animals there.
body:
The Metternich Stela, dated to the 30th Dynasty in the 4th century BC, records this spell in section I. Its purpose is described as protection on water. The formula is a four-part disabling statement involving the mouth, maw, tongue, and eyes.

In sequence, the mouth is shut by the Sun, the maw is plugged by Sekhmet, the tongue is cut out by Thoth, and the eyes are blinded by Magic. The formula then declares that the four great gods make protection for every person and animal on the water. Its logic is to close hostile faculties through distinct divine powers before stating a wider protective result.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this can be understood as a tightly ordered lesson in protection: disable harmful speech, appetite, language, and sight, then affirm safety for all on the water. The record does not explain how the formula was performed beyond its stated sequence, so its exact historical use remains uncertain. As a study text, it also shows how protection could be expressed through several linked divine actions rather than one general appeal.
reflection: What changes when protection is imagined as the closing of specific hostile faculties before it is extended to every person and animal on the water?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the historical rite, read the four-part sequence silently and write a brief note about the kinds of harmful influence that the images of closed mouth, maw, tongue, and eyes suggest to you.
sourceCitation: Metternich Stela (Metropolitan Museum of Art 50.85) - Metternich Stela, section I, Spell for protection on water

title: Barley Bread Kneaded with Salt
intro: This lesson examines a historical healing dressing recorded in the Metternich Stela. It combines barley bread, salt, spoken recitation, and a bandage applied to an affected place, with garlic associated with the burning sensation.
body:
The Metternich Stela, from the 30th Dynasty in the 4th century BC, records this dressing within a long Isis narrative. Borghouts spell 91 describes barley bread kneaded with salt, a spell recited over it, and the prepared bread applied as a bandage to the affected place. The text pairs this treatment with garlic for a burning sensation.

In its own terms, the procedure joined material treatment with spoken words. The bread and salt formed the dressing, while recitation gave the preparation its ritual role. Garlic's heat was credited with driving out the burning pain, linking a physical quality to the desired relief.

What is documented ends there: the text records the ingredients, recitation, application, and attributed purpose. Read now, this entry can show how healing was framed through both a physical covering and spoken ritual action. Whether such a dressing relieved symptoms in practice remains uncertain. The record does not provide further medical explanation or evidence of its results.
reflection: How does the pairing of a physical bandage, spoken recitation, and garlic's credited heat shape your understanding of what healing meant in this text?
practice: As a modern study practice, read this entry aloud and journal about the different roles assigned to the bread, salt, recitation, and bandage. This is a reflection exercise, not a reconstruction of the historical rite.
safetyNote: The historical procedure is recorded for study and must not be attempted. Bites, stings, and infections can be medical emergencies; seek appropriate medical treatment.
sourceCitation: Metternich Stela (Metropolitan Museum of Art 50.85) - Borghouts spell 91 (Metternich Stela, 108-251)

title: Garlic and Beer for the House
intro: This lesson examines a house-protection preparation recorded on a stela of Wennofer. The preparation uses garlic and beer, applied through the rooms at night to guard the household.
body:
The source is a stela in the Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek, identified as A 13N 974. Borghouts spell 121 records grinding garlic together with beer and sprinkling the mixture through the house during the night, before daybreak. The stated threats include snakes, scorpions, reptiles, and the hostile dead. The text belongs to the Ancient Egyptian tradition and is dated to the Late Period, 664-332 BC.

In its own terms, the preparation worked by placing a protective substance throughout the rooms at a particular time. Garlic and beer were combined, then distributed across the household before daylight. The action connected the material mixture, the boundaries of the house, and the night-time period with the aim of keeping harmful beings outside.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this rite can be studied as a focused example of how household protection joined ordinary materials with a timed act of covering domestic space. It remains uncertain whether the preparation was understood as symbolic, physically effective, or both, and the record does not explain how often it was performed or by whom.
reflection: What does the movement from grinding the mixture to sprinkling it through every room suggest about how protection was imagined within the household?
practice: As a modern study practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, read the entry aloud and write down which parts of your home you think of as needing care or protection. Do not make or sprinkle the historical mixture.
safetyNote: The historical procedure is recorded for study and must not be attempted. Garlic and beer should not be used as a protective household preparation, and any modern household practice should avoid creating spills or attracting pests.
sourceCitation: Stela in the Ny Carlsberg Glyptothek A 13N 974 - Borghouts spell 121 (Ny Carlsberg Glyptothek, A 13N 974)

title: Herbs in Beer and Myrrh After a Nightmare
intro: This lesson examines the material part of an Ancient Egyptian spell intended to address a nightmare. The record combines bread given in the practitioner's presence with fresh herbs soaked in beer and myrrh.
body:
Borghouts, Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts records this procedure as spell 7 in P. Chester Beatty III, recto 10, 6-9. The text belongs to the Ancient Egyptian tradition of the New Kingdom, c. 1550-1070 BC. It describes bread being given to the sufferer in the practitioner's presence, followed by fresh herbs soaked in beer and myrrh and rubbed over the dreamer's face while the spell was recited.

In its own terms, the spoken spell and the physical actions belonged together. Food was provided in a witnessed setting, while the scented mixture was placed directly on the face. The record presents these actions as the material part of the nightmare spell, but it does not explain the separate power or meaning assigned to the bread, beer, herbs, or myrrh.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this entry can be approached as evidence of how words, food, scent, and touch were joined in an ancient response to distressing dreams. What remains uncertain is how the original practitioners understood the specific role of each material. This is a historical reconstruction for study and reading, not a modern prescription.
reflection: What might the pairing of spoken words with food, scent, and touch have communicated to someone seeking relief after a nightmare?
practice: As a modern reflective practice, write down a nightmare and note the sensory details that remain with you, such as taste, scent, or touch. Read the historical description aloud as a study exercise, without attempting to reproduce the procedure.
safetyNote: The historical procedure involves fresh herbs, myrrh, beer, and application to the face. It is recorded for study and must not be attempted; do not apply historical mixtures to skin or face.
sourceCitation: Borghouts, Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts - Borghouts spell 7 (P. Chester Beatty III, recto 10, 6-9)

title: Oil Recited Over Seven Times for Fever
intro: This lesson examines a fever treatment recorded in the Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden. The procedure uses genuine oil, spoken words, and anointing connected with Isis, Nephthys, and Horus son of Isis.
body:
The Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden records a fever treatment requiring only genuine oil. The formula is recited seven times over the oil. The source is identified as Graeco-Roman Egypt and dated to the 3rd century AD, at P. London-Leiden, verso col. XXXIII, 1-9.

In its own terms, the spoken formula gives the oil its role in the treatment. Isis, Nephthys, and Horus son of Isis are invoked during the recitation. The treated oil is then used to anoint the patient's hand, body, and feet, while the words are spoken to the patient as the work proceeds.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this entry shows a healing procedure in which repeated speech, divine invocation, oil, touch, and direct address were joined into one act of care. The record does not establish whether the treatment relieved fever, so its practical effect remains uncertain. Its value for study lies in preserving how this handbook presented the treatment, not in confirming it as medicine.
reflection: What might the combination of repeated speech, anointing, and direct attention to the patient have expressed about care in this historical setting?
practice: As a modern practice, write a short journal entry describing the sequence of this historical treatment and what its use of voice, oil, and touch suggests to you. This is a reflection exercise, not a reconstruction or medical treatment.
safetyNote: The historical procedure is recorded for study and must not be attempted. Bites, stings, and infections are medical emergencies; seek treatment.
sourceCitation: Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden - P. London-Leiden, verso col. XXXIII, 1-9

title: A Ritual in the Royal Court
intro: This lesson examines Maqlu as a text used in an actual royal setting, not only as literature. A letter from the exorcist Nabu-nadin-shumi to the Assyrian king Esarhaddon places the ceremony within court practice.
body:
Maqlu is discussed in a letter between the exorcist Nabu-nadin-shumi and the Assyrian king Esarhaddon. The correspondence shows that the ceremony was being scheduled and discussed for the king during the 7th century BC. This connects the work studied by scribes with a real event in royal life.

In its own terms, the evidence presents ritual knowledge as something that could move between written study and practical performance. The text was not treated as literature alone. An exorcist was involved, and the ceremony had a place in court planning, showing that its use required organization and attention to timing.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this letter invites attention to the moment when written tradition becomes planned action, without allowing us to fill in details that the record does not provide. It remains uncertain what the full ceremony involved and how it was carried out. The surviving evidence is especially valuable because it records use, not merely preservation or study.
reflection: How does knowing that Maqlu was scheduled for a king change the way you understand the relationship between scribal learning and ritual practice?
practice: As a modern study practice, write a short journal entry distinguishing what the record documents from what you would only be guessing about the ceremony. Read your summary aloud as a reminder to keep historical evidence and personal interpretation separate.
sourceCitation: Maqlu - Letter of the exorcist Nabu-nadin-shumi to Esarhaddon

title: A Secret of the House of Life
intro: This lesson examines a restriction recorded within the Harris Magical Papyrus. The passage shows that the transmission of magical knowledge could be limited to trained personnel connected with the House of Life.
body:
The Harris Magical Papyrus records a water spell with an attached restriction clause. The chief lectors say, "Do not reveal it to others. A veritable secret of the House of Life." The passage is from the recto, column 6/10, section K, and belongs to the 20th Dynasty.

In its own terms, the spell's knowledge was not treated as open instruction. The restriction identifies who could transmit it and presents the teaching as a secret held within the House of Life. This indicates that the text circulated among trained temple personnel rather than freely among all readers.

What is documented ends there: the passage records the secrecy rule and its institutional setting, but it does not explain every reason for the restriction or how widely the rule was followed. Read now, this entry can prompt reflection on how authority is created by controlling access to specialized knowledge. The wording makes secrecy part of the text itself, rather than a later rule imposed by modern readers. What remains uncertain is the full practical process by which this particular spell was taught and transmitted.
reflection: What does the restriction in this passage suggest about the relationship between specialized knowledge, authority, and responsibility within the House of Life?
practice: As a modern practice, write a short journal entry about one kind of knowledge you consider private, and explain what respectful transmission of it would require. This is a reflection exercise, not a reconstruction of the historical spell.
sourceCitation: Harris Magical Papyrus (BM EA 10042) - Harris Magical Papyrus, recto col. 6/10, section K (Lange 1927: 53-54)

title: Cosmic Blackmail
intro: This lesson examines a rhetorical method in Ancient Egyptian magical texts: naming a consequence so severe that a god is pressured to grant a smaller request. The examples include a birth-related spell and a love charm.
body:
Borghouts records this strategy in spell 63, preserved in Papyrus Berlin 3027, and in spell 1, preserved in ODeM 1057. In the first example, the text threatens the loss of heaven, earth, offerings, sunlight, and the inundation if Isis does not give birth. The second is a love charm that threatens to burn Busiris and Osiris himself.

In its own terms, the practitioner creates leverage by presenting the requested result as the cheaper choice. The gods are not simply asked to act; they are confronted with consequences so intolerable that granting the smaller request becomes the more reasonable option. The method turns a personal aim into a crisis for the wider universe or for powerful divine figures.

What is documented ends there: these texts preserve the threat structure and its intended magical logic, not proof that such threats produced their stated results. Read now, this material can be studied as an extreme example of persuasive language, in which urgency and scale are used to strengthen a demand. It remains uncertain how different practitioners or audiences understood the literal force of these threats.
reflection: When a request is framed as a crisis for everyone, what does that reveal about the power and limits the speaker feels they have?
practice: As a modern practice, write one non-coercive request for yourself and name a realistic consequence of leaving it unaddressed. Keep the exercise focused on clarifying priorities, not on threatening or controlling another person.
sourceCitation: Borghouts, Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts - Borghouts spell 63 (Papyrus Berlin 3027, verso 3, 8-4, 3); spell 1 (ODeM 1057)

title: Girra and Nusku
intro: This lesson examines the distinct roles of Nusku and Girra in the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. Both are connected with fire, but the text assigns them different tasks in the ritual.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records incantation openings addressed separately to Nusku and Girra. Its 7th century BC manuscripts describe Nusku as the night lamp and messenger, called offspring of Anu and counsellor of the great gods. Girra is addressed as blazing, powerful, and a wild fire-storm.

In the ritual's own terms, Nusku carries the case and guards the dark, while Girra carries out the sentence. The openings also identify which power is being addressed for which figurine material. This distinction gives the two fire powers separate functions rather than treating them as interchangeable forms of fire.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this lesson can be understood as a study of divided roles: one power carries and protects, while the other performs the final act. The record does not explain every figurine material or provide a modern interpretation of what each sentence meant. It remains uncertain how practitioners understood the full relationship between the two powers beyond these assigned ritual tasks.
reflection: When you separate Nusku's work of carrying and guarding from Girra's work of execution, what difference does that make to your understanding of fire as a ritual power?
practice: As a modern study practice, write two headings, Nusku and Girra, and place the documented roles beneath each one. Read the distinction aloud without using flame or attempting to reconstruct the rite.
safetyNote: The historical material involves fire and is recorded here for study, not as a procedure to recreate. Do not use flame or attempt to perform the historical ritual.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 26'-41' (Nusku and Girra incipits)

title: How the Text Survived
intro: This lesson follows how Maqlu has survived through tablets, fragments, and copies made in scribal training. It focuses on the libraries and student materials that help scholars reconstruct the text.
body:
Maqlu reaches the present through more than a hundred cuneiform tablets and fragments. The surviving materials include copies from the royal libraries of Nineveh, the private library of the exorcist Kisir-Assur at Ashur, the library of Iqisa at Uruk in the 4th-3rd century, and student copies made during training. The manuscripts belong to the 7th-3rd century BC range recorded for this tradition.

The incantations were part of the scribal curriculum, so apprentices copied them while learning. These student copies are important because they can preserve lines that are lost from the master manuscripts. Comparing materials from different libraries and stages of training allows the text to be studied as a transmitted work rather than as one surviving copy.

What is documented ends there: the manuscripts show how Maqlu was copied and preserved, not every detail of how each historical practitioner used it. Read now, this history presents preservation as a distributed process involving royal collections, private libraries, and student work. It remains uncertain or debated how individual copies relate to one another beyond the general evidence that apprentice copies help reconstruct missing lines.
reflection: How might your understanding of Maqlu change when you consider student copies as part of the text's survival rather than treating them as lesser versions?
practice: As a modern study practice, read a student excerpt alongside another available excerpt and journal what appears repeated, missing, or changed. This is a reading exercise, not a reconstruction of the historical rite.
sourceCitation: Corpus of Mesopotamian Anti-witchcraft Rituals (CMAwRo) - Schwemer, Maqlu overview: manuscripts and libraries

title: How to Dismiss What You Called
intro: This lesson examines the closing procedure recorded after a vessel-divination in the Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden. It focuses on dismissal as a defined part of the working, not an optional ending.
body:
The Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden, a Graeco-Roman Egyptian source from the 3rd century AD, includes an exit procedure after vessel-divination. In P. London-Leiden, col. III, 28-30, a fumigant is burned and a dismissal is spoken: "Good dispatch, joyful dispatch!" The stated purpose is for every entity to depart to its place.

In the terms of the handbook, the working has boundaries at both ends. The invocation begins the operation, while the fumigant and spoken dismissal bring it to a specified close. The ending is therefore part of the method itself, with the words directing all entities away rather than leaving the divination open.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this passage highlights the importance the handbook places on closure after vessel-divination. It can also be read as a reminder that a ritual's conclusion may carry its own instructions and meaning. It remains uncertain how practitioners understood the entities involved beyond what this brief record states, and the text does not provide a modern explanation for the procedure.
reflection: How does treating the dismissal as carefully specified as the invocation change the way you think about ending a focused or uncertain activity?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, write a short closing sentence after today's reading or reflection. Read it aloud to mark that the activity is complete, without burning a fumigant or attempting the historical procedure.
safetyNote: The historical account involves a burned fumigant and smoke. It is recorded here for study and should not be attempted; use reading or writing instead of flame, smoke, or fumigants.
sourceCitation: Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden - P. London-Leiden, col. III, 28-30

title: Materials Chosen for How They Die
intro: This lesson examines why different substances were selected for figurines in the Mesopotamian Maqlu ritual. Their behavior in flame gave each material a distinct way of representing an ending.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records figurine materials by incantation in obv. 23'-41'. The listed substances include tamarisk, cedar, tallow, wax, sesame pomace, bitumen, gypsum, clay, and dough. The source belongs to the Mesopotamian Akkadian and Standard Babylonian tradition, preserved in 7th century BC manuscripts.

In the ritual's own terms, the substance was part of the argument. Clay could burst in fire, while tallow and wax could melt. Bitumen and sesame pomace could burn foully. These different outcomes made destruction visible in different ways, so the material was not merely decorative.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this entry suggests a focused way to study symbolic action: observe what an object does, then ask what kind of ending that behavior expresses. The record does not explain every material's role or establish how practitioners debated these choices, so the full meaning of tamarisk, cedar, gypsum, and dough remains uncertain. The surviving description supports the principle that material behavior carried meaning, but not every interpretation of the list.
reflection: If each material was chosen for the kind of ending it enacted, which form of change would you associate with melting, bursting, or foul burning, and why?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, copy the nine-material list into a journal. Beside each substance, note only the documented behavior where one is given, and leave the others marked as uncertain.
safetyNote: The historical procedure involves flame, smoke, and burning materials. It is recorded here for study and must not be attempted; do not burn these substances.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 23'-41' (figurine materials by incantation)

title: Names from Everywhere
intro: This lesson examines how the Theban handbooks combine names from several religious traditions in their invocation lists. The source is the Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden, from Graeco-Roman Egypt in the 3rd century AD.
body:
The Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden records invocation lists that place Egyptian, Greek, Hebrew, and Mesopotamian names together. Anubis and Osiris appear beside Iaho, Sabaho, Adonai, Ereskhigal, Abraham, and Agathodaemon. These passages are cited from P. London-Leiden, col. VIII, 1-11 and verso XV, 1-7.

In the terms of the handbooks, the list gains force through accumulation. More names meant wider coverage, so the text did not need to choose one pantheon or make every tradition agree. Contradictions between the names were not treated as a problem that needed to be solved.

Read now, this list shows a practical way of building authority through breadth rather than consistency. Its mixture can be studied as a deliberate joining of names from different traditions within one invocation. What remains uncertain is how every individual name was understood by each practitioner or reader. The record does not require the pantheon to be resolved before the list can be understood as an accumulating form of coverage.
reflection: What changes in your reading when you treat the mixed names as an intentional accumulation rather than as a system that must be made internally consistent?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the listed names silently and write down what the sequence suggests about accumulation and coverage. This is a reading and journalling exercise, not a reconstruction of the historical invocation.
sourceCitation: Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden - P. London-Leiden, col. VIII, 1-11; verso XV, 1-7

title: Power in a Foreign Tongue
intro: This lesson examines foreign-language incantations recorded in the London Medical Papyrus. The passage concerns seven formulas against skin disease and shows how unfamiliar speech could be treated as a source of power.
body:
The London Medical Papyrus preserves a run of seven incantations against skin conditions. Six are written in a Northwest Semitic language, while one is labelled as the tongue of Crete. The record also notes that Nubian names and formulas were used in the same way.

In the practitioners' terms, the foreign sound was deliberate. Its strangeness was considered effective in itself, so an untranslatable spell did not necessarily indicate confusion or misunderstanding. Imported language could function as a powerful part of the healing formula.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this passage invites attention to how unfamiliar language can be given authority within a ritual system, especially when its meaning is not available to everyone present. It remains uncertain how each formula was spoken, understood, or used in practice, because the record provides no further detail here.
reflection: What might make an unfamiliar language feel powerful or authoritative in a healing context, even when its meaning is uncertain?
practice: As a modern practice, read a short familiar text and then notice your response to hearing an unfamiliar language, without treating either as medical treatment. Write down how sound, meaning, and strangeness affect your attention.
safetyNote: The historical material concerns skin disease and is recorded for study, not as a medical treatment. Do not use these incantations in place of appropriate care for skin symptoms.
sourceCitation: London Medical Papyrus (BM EA 10059) - London Medical Papyrus, seven incantations against skin conditions; Guide to the Study of Ancient Magic

title: Tests and Prognoses
intro: This lesson examines procedures in the Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden for finding things out. The procedures offer prognoses, including a pregnancy test and a divination involving which of a boy's ears responds.
body:
The Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden preserves a pregnancy test in which a woman urinates on a plant. It also records a divination that observes which of a boy's ears responds. These procedures belong to Graeco-Roman Egypt and are dated to the 3rd century AD.

In their own terms, the procedures were tests rather than treatments. The plant's condition supplied a yes or no: if it was scorched, the result meant no conception; if it flourished, the result meant conception. The ear procedure likewise used a response to produce an answer. Their form is empirical in that an observable result was used to reach a conclusion, even though the underlying premise is not established here.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this lesson invites a careful distinction between prognosis and treatment: learning what was believed to be happening is not the same as curing it. The surviving record does not establish how often these procedures were used, how reliable they were considered, or how the ear divination was interpreted in every case. Their historical value lies in showing how observation and stated rules could be joined in a search for certainty.
reflection: What changes when you separate the desire to know an outcome from the expectation that knowledge should also provide a cure?
practice: As a modern practice, write one question you want answered and two separate notes: one describing what evidence might inform it, and another describing what action, if any, would follow. Treat the exercise as reflection, not as a reconstruction of the historical procedures.
safetyNote: The historical material includes a pregnancy-related procedure and the use of a plant. It is recorded for study and must not be attempted; modern pregnancy questions should be addressed with appropriate current medical testing and care.
sourceCitation: Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden - P. London-Leiden, verso col. V, 4-8; col. III, 16-20

title: The Child Medium
intro: This lesson examines a vessel and lamp divination procedure recorded in the Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden. The procedure depends on testing a boy as the medium through whom answers may be received.
body:
The London-Leiden handbook, from Graeco-Roman Egypt in the 3rd century AD, records the use of a boy who had not been with a woman. He was tested, dressed in clean linen, seated on a new brick, and prepared for vessel or lamp divination. The relevant passages appear in P. London-Leiden, col. III, 11-20 and col. X, 9-22.

In the procedure's own terms, the boy's responses showed whether he was suitable. The operator recited the spell into his head seven times, then judged which ear answered. An answer from both ears was considered very good, the right ear good, and the left ear bad. The ear response served as the test by which the medium was accepted or rejected.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this lesson shows a tightly controlled selection process in which clothing, seating, repetition, and bodily response were treated as meaningful signs. The record does not explain how the boy's responses were produced or whether the procedure was understood in other ways. Its historical use is documented, but its claimed divinatory effectiveness remains uncertain.
reflection: What might the emphasis on testing, repeated recitation, and the boy's answering ear reveal about how practitioners defined reliability in a medium?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, read the record once and journal which details establish its test of suitability. Note what the text states directly and what it leaves unexplained.
safetyNote: The historical procedure involves a child and is recorded for study; it must not be attempted. Do not recruit or test a child as a medium.
sourceCitation: Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden - P. London-Leiden, col. III, 11-20; col. X, 9-22

title: The Figurine as Legal Substitute
intro: This lesson examines two roles assigned to images in the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. An image may represent the sorcerer and be destroyed, or it may represent a substitute for the patient and be washed over before being discarded.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records a "figurine of the substitute" in two passages. In this use, the patient washes his hands over the figurine. The source also distinguishes this image from a figurine representing the sorcerer, which is destroyed.

Within the ritual's own logic, an image could stand in for a person. A substitute figurine represented the patient and received the contamination directed at him. Washing the hands over it transferred the unwanted condition to the substitute, which was then discarded. The sorcerer's likeness had a different function and was treated as an object to destroy.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this lesson highlights how the same kind of object could have different meanings depending on whom it represented. What remains uncertain is how every practitioner understood the figurines or how consistently these distinctions were applied beyond the recorded passages. The important documented contrast is between destroying an enemy image and discarding a substitute after washing over it.
reflection: How does the meaning of an image change when it represents the source of harm rather than the person seeking relief?
practice: As a modern study practice, make two small paper labels: "sorcerer" and "substitute." Place them apart and write one sentence describing the different role assigned to each image in the Maqlu passage. Do not treat this as a reconstruction of the historical rite.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 150'-151'

title: The Theban Magical Library
intro: This lesson examines the London-Leiden handbook as part of a multilingual group of Graeco-Roman Egyptian magical books found together at Thebes. It focuses on how one working appears across Demotic and Greek forms.
body:
The London-Leiden handbook belongs to a group of magical books found together at Thebes. It runs for 29 columns on the recto and 33 on the verso, and is written mostly in Demotic, with Greek and Old Coptic material alongside a cipher script. The source is the Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden, associated with the 3rd century AD and PDM xiv.

The record shows that magical knowledge in this library could be layered across languages and scripts. A Demotic passage in London-Leiden, PDM xiv.627-635, is closely translated in a Greek spell, PGM IV.1-25. In its own terms, the connection suggests that the same working circulated in more than one written form within the wider library.

What is documented ends there: the record demonstrates textual connection, but does not explain how every reader used each script or how the cipher material functioned. Read now, this library can be understood as a place where magical learning was preserved through multilingual transmission rather than through one fixed language alone. It remains uncertain from this record how closely the surviving versions matched in actual performance.
reflection: How does seeing one working move between Demotic and Greek change your sense of what it meant to preserve magical knowledge in the Theban library?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the lesson once and write a short journal entry comparing the roles of Demotic, Greek, Old Coptic, and cipher script in the record. This is a reflection on textual transmission, not a reconstruction of the historical working.
sourceCitation: Griffith & Thompson, The Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden (1904-1909); PDM xiv

title: Threatening the Tools
intro: This lesson examines a Graeco-Egyptian technique in which a lamp-wick is addressed as a participant in the work. The example comes from the Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden, from 3rd century AD Graeco-Roman Egypt.
body:
The Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden records an address to a lamp-wick in P. London-Leiden, col. VI, 11-21. The wick is called the linen of Thoth and the bandage of Osiris, and it is warned: "If thou wilt not do it, I will not give thee oil."

In the terms of the practice, the wick is treated as a party with an interest of its own. Since it wants oil, the operator has leverage over it. The threat is therefore presented as a method of bargaining with equipment, rather than simply as disrespect toward an object.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this can be studied as a model of ritual speech that gives a tool a role, a need, and a reason to comply. It may also invite reflection on how authority is created through naming and conditional promises. It remains uncertain from this record whether the wick was understood as literally aware or whether this was primarily a practical ritual way of speaking to it.
reflection: When you address an ordinary tool as though it had an interest in cooperating, what changes in your attention to the tool and to your own intentions?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, choose one safe everyday object and write two sentences describing its function and what would help you use it well. Read the sentences aloud without treating the object as literally conscious.
safetyNote: The historical material involves a lamp and oil. Any procedure involving flame is recorded here for study and must not be attempted.
sourceCitation: Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden - P. London-Leiden, col. VI, 11-21

title: Traces of a Person
intro: This lesson examines contact and personal traces in the Mesopotamian anti-witchcraft text Maqlu. It focuses on how discarded, intimate, or trodden-on matter was treated as a link to a person, and how the counter-ritual answered that logic.
body:
Maqlu records a form of Babylonian witchcraft that worked through contact. The examples include river clay shaped into an image, water buried in a tomb, scraps from a dust-heap, a fringe torn at the fuller's house, and dirt from a threshold that had been walked on. These materials were treated as pieces of the victim's life.

In its own terms, the material did not need to be the person themselves. A discarded object, an intimate fragment, or matter touched by the person could serve as a handle for working against them. The counter-ritual answered by identifying each stolen link and finding equivalent matter for an image of the witch.

What is documented ends there: the passage shows the logic of contact and the structure of the counter-ritual, but it does not explain every practical detail or establish how practitioners judged the ritual's results. Read now, this lesson can prompt attention to how ordinary objects become charged with personal meaning. It also invites careful distinction between historical belief and modern interpretation.
reflection: Which kinds of discarded, intimate, or trodden-on objects feel most strongly connected to a person in your own experience, and why?
practice: As a modern reflective practice, write three categories of personal traces: discarded, intimate, and trodden-on. Beside each, note one ordinary object that carries personal meaning for you, without treating the exercise as a reconstruction of the historical rite.
sourceCitation: Maqlu VII, 183-192

title: Witchcraft as a Lawsuit
intro: This lesson examines Maqlu as a legal reversal of a harmful judgment. The ritual presents the patient as wrongly condemned and the sorcerers as responsible for the accusation.
body:
The Corpus of Mesopotamian Anti-witchcraft Rituals records Maqlu as a ritual in which the patient's death sentence is understood to have been obtained through the sorcerers' slander. In this setting, the ritual acts as a retrial that overturns the earlier verdict. The material belongs to the Mesopotamian Akkadian or Standard Babylonian tradition and is associated with the 1st millennium BC.

In its own terms, the ritual uses the language of law. The gods are addressed as a court, the patient is treated as a defendant who was wrongly convicted, and the sorcerers are treated as perjurers. The fire is understood not as personal revenge but as sentencing: the fate prepared for the patient is returned to those who engineered it.

What is documented ends there; the record describes the ritual's legal framing, but it does not establish how later readers should apply that framework today. Read now, this lesson can present justice as the correction of a false accusation rather than as uncontrolled retaliation. The exact historical performance and the full range of its meanings remain uncertain from this record alone.
reflection: When a harmful accusation is imagined as a wrongful verdict, what would a fair retrial need to restore before judgment could be reversed?
practice: As a modern practice, write a short, neutral account of a situation in which blame may have been assigned too quickly. Divide the page into accusation, evidence, and a fairer revised judgment, without naming or targeting another person.
safetyNote: The historical material uses fire as part of its ritual imagery. Do not recreate the historical procedure or use fire as a means of judgment; the modern exercise should remain written and symbolic.
sourceCitation: Corpus of Mesopotamian Anti-witchcraft Rituals (CMAwRo) - Schwemer, Maqlu overview: ritual as legal process

title: Writing and Drawing as Delivery
intro: This lesson examines Egyptian spells in which writing and drawing were applied to the body rather than only spoken. The source records figures, written names, materials, and points of contact as parts of the procedure.
body:
Borghouts records several Egyptian applications of this kind. In one spell, a figure is drawn on fine linen and laid on the throat. Another has the names of seven spirits written out. A further spell has a figure of Re drawn in fish blood and placed on the head. These examples are cited from Borghouts, Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts, including spells 6, 8, and 40.

In the practitioners' terms, the image or text itself acted as a physical medicine. The drawn figure was treated as the dose. This is why the entries specify the surface, the pigment, and the part of the body that the material touched. The application was therefore not separate from the writing or drawing; it was the central operation.

What is documented ends there: the record describes the materials and their placement, but does not provide a modern medical explanation or establish an outcome. Read now, this lesson highlights how meaning could be assigned through the precise handling of an image, a written name, and a bodily location. It remains uncertain how every practitioner understood the relationship between the figure, its material, and its effect.
reflection: What changes in your understanding of a written or drawn symbol when the surface, pigment, and place of bodily contact are treated as essential parts of it?
practice: As a modern study practice, draw a simple abstract figure on ordinary paper and write beside it the surface, material, and point of contact described in this entry. Do not place it on your body or use the historical materials; simply journal about how the instructions shape your reading.
safetyNote: The historical procedures are recorded for study and must not be attempted. In particular, do not use fish blood or place drawn materials on the body.
sourceCitation: Borghouts, Ancient Egyptian Magical Texts - Borghouts spell 6 (P. Leiden I 348, verso 2), spell 8 (P. Chester Beatty VI, verso 2, 5-9), spell 40 (P. Leiden I 348, recto 6, 4-8, 7)

title: Ban, Ban: The Circle Around the Bed
intro: This lesson examines a short protective act from the Mesopotamian Maqlu Ritual Tablet. It centers on drawing a circle around a bed and reciting two brief incantations near the end of the night.
body:
The record comes from the Mesopotamian tradition, in Akkadian and Standard Babylonian, preserved in 7th century BC manuscripts and cited as Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obverse lines 136 to 137. It records two very short incantations spoken near the end of the night while a circle is drawn around the bed, one beginning with a doubled ban and one declaring the house adjured.

In its own terms the act works by enclosure and by oath. The drawn circle marks the sleeping place as a bounded space, and the spoken adjuration puts the whole house under a binding word, so the protection is both a line on the ground and a legal-sounding claim over the dwelling. Its placement late in the night sequence matters: it guards the hours when the patient can do nothing for himself.

What is documented ends there. Read now, the pairing of a drawn line with a spoken oath is a reminder that these rites protected a place and a person at once, not just a body. What remains uncertain is how large the circle was, what it was drawn with, and whether the same person who recited also drew it, because the tablet records only the cue lines and not the stage directions.
reflection: What might the image of a circled bed and a house placed under oath reveal about the kinds of safety a household sought at night?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, draw or write a simple circle on paper around the words bed and home. Read the two recorded phrases aloud as historical text, then note what the boundary symbolizes for you today.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 136'-137'

title: Black Liquid on the Fate-Goddess
intro: This lesson examines a harsh reversal described in the Maqlu burning sequence. It centers on a figurine representing a witch's personal fate-goddess and the defilement of that figure with black liquid.
body:
The Maqlu is a Mesopotamian text in Akkadian or Standard Babylonian, dated in the record to the 1st millennium BC. In this sequence, a figurine representing the witch's personal fate-goddess is set up, and black liquid is poured over its head. The sufferer then leaves the figurine behind in the darkness of night. The entry is also discussed in Schwemer's CMAwRo overview.

Within the ritual's own terms, the fate-goddess protects and shapes the witch's destiny. Fouling the figure's head was therefore understood to foul that protection and seal the witch's evil fate and death. The act worked through reversal: the figure of the witch's protecting fate became the target of the harmful action.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this scene can be studied as an example of how ritual objects were used to represent a person's protection, destiny, and vulnerability. The record does not explain every detail of the black liquid or establish how every practitioner understood the act, so those points remain uncertain. This entry is a historical reconstruction for study, not a modern prescription.
reflection: What does the use of a fate-goddess figurine suggest about the connection between protection, identity, and destiny in this ritual?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, write down one harmful pattern or fear you want to leave behind. Read the sentence aloud, then place the paper in a journal or folder as a reminder of reflection rather than an action against anyone.
sourceCitation: Maqlu, burning sequence; Schwemer, CMAwRo overview

title: Coloured Twine Around the Bed
intro: This lesson examines a minimal boundary rite recorded in the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. It uses coloured twine to mark the sleeping place as an enclosed area during sleep.
body:
The source is the Maqlu Ritual Tablet, a Mesopotamian text in Akkadian or Standard Babylonian tradition. The cited passage is on obv. 117', and the surviving manuscripts belong to the 7th century BC. The entry records one action: surrounding the bed with coloured twine so that the sleeping place is enclosed.

In its own terms, the rite worked by creating a visible and marked perimeter around the bed. Sleep was treated as a vulnerable period, and the enclosed boundary distinguished the sleeping place from the surrounding space. The record does not explain which colour was used, what the colours meant, or whether spoken words accompanied the act.

What is documented ends there. Read now, the rite can be understood as a focused act of marking personal space before sleep, while avoiding claims about meanings the entry does not provide. What remains uncertain is the specific significance of the coloured twine and the full ritual context of the cited passage. This entry is a historical reconstruction for study and reading, not a modern prescription.
reflection: What kind of boundary would help you feel that your sleeping space has been intentionally set apart from the concerns of the day?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, place a visible ribbon or piece of cord beside your bed as a reminder to set aside the day's concerns before sleep. Do not encircle the bed if the material could create a tripping hazard.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 117'

title: Conjuration in the Speech of Keftiu
intro: This lesson examines an Egyptian incantation against the Asiatic disease from the London Medical Papyrus. The formula is labeled as being in the speech of Keftiu, described in the record as the Cretan tongue.
body:
The London Medical Papyrus preserves a conjuration against the Asiatic disease from the Late 18th-19th Dynasty, around 1350-1300 BC. The text records the foreign-language formula as s-n-t-k-p-p-wy-i-y-m-n-t-r-k-k-r and preserves its sounds rather than an Egyptian meaning.

In its own terms, the formula was spoken over a prepared remedy base. That base was then applied to the affected part. The use of a foreign speech was part of the spell's force, since the record describes the power of these formulas as lying partly in their unintelligibility.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this text shows how sound, foreignness, and treatment were joined within an ancient healing practice. The formula's original meaning and precise pronunciation remain uncertain from this record. For modern readers, its value is as evidence of how language itself could be treated as an active element in a remedy.
reflection: What might the use of an unintelligible foreign formula have communicated to a person seeking relief from illness?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the recorded transliteration aloud once while keeping it separate from any remedy or medical treatment. Notice how its unfamiliar sounds affect your attention, without treating the reading as a reconstruction or prescription.
safetyNote: The historical procedure is recorded for study and must not be attempted as a medical treatment. Do not apply remedies based on this entry to an affected body part; seek qualified medical care for illness.
sourceCitation: London Medical Papyrus (BM EA 10059) - London Medical Papyrus, conjuration of the Asiatic disease in the speech of Keftiu

title: Ea Has Unbound the Sinews
intro: This lesson examines a short unbinding rite from the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. It invokes Ea, described in the record as a god of water and wisdom, while a crucible's contents are stirred with a cornel stick.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records an instruction to stir the contents of a crucible with a stick of cornel. While stirring, the practitioner recites, "Ea has now unbound the sinews that you have bound up." The passage is cited as Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 81'-82', in 7th century BC manuscripts from the Mesopotamian Akkadian or Standard Babylonian tradition.

Within the rite's own terms, the action joins movement, material, and speech. Stirring the crucible represents loosening, while the words name Ea as the power that unbinds what has been tied. The image of bound sinews gives the act a bodily sense, even though the record does not explain the condition further.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this passage can be considered a focused image of release: a spoken declaration accompanies the deliberate stirring of something held together. What remains uncertain is how the original practitioners understood the bound condition or what they believed the rite changed beyond this recorded action. This entry is a historical reconstruction for study and reading, not a modern prescription.
reflection: When something feels tightly bound in your life, what would it mean to name release without assuming that you know exactly what caused the binding?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, write the words "Ea has now unbound the sinews that you have bound up" in a journal, then note what kind of release the image brings to mind. Do not use a crucible, cornel, or other ritual materials.
safetyNote: The historical account mentions a cornel stick and a crucible. This entry is for study, and the recorded procedure should not be recreated; avoid handling or preparing plants for this purpose.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 81'-82'

title: First Spell of Enchanting All That Is in the Water
intro: This lesson examines a river-protection text from the Harris Magical Papyrus. It records a restricted rite associated with a lector priest working over water before crossing or working on the river.
body:
The text comes from the Harris Magical Papyrus, dated to the 19th-20th Dynasty, around 1200-1100 BC. It is identified as the First Spell of Enchanting All That Is in the Water and was transmitted within the temple House of Life. The chief lectors caution, "Do not reveal it to others. A veritable secret of the House of Life."

In its own terms, the rite was recited by a lector priest over water. Its purpose was to bind everything living in the water before the priest crossed or worked on the river. The record specifically tags the spell with water, crocodile, secrecy, and lector priest, presenting spoken enchantment as the means of securing passage or activity on the river.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this text can be studied as an example of how restricted knowledge and verbal action were connected to protection in a particular setting. The record does not establish how the binding was understood in detail, how it affected living creatures, or how the rite was performed beyond its recitation over water. This entry is a historical reconstruction for study, not a modern prescription.
reflection: What does the text's secrecy clause suggest to you about the relationship between protection, authority, and restricted knowledge in the House of Life?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the entry quietly and journal about the boundaries you want to observe when approaching water. Do not treat this as a reconstruction of the historical rite.
safetyNote: The historical procedure is recorded for study and must not be attempted, especially not on wildlife or in natural water. The reference to binding living creatures should remain part of historical reading rather than modern practice.
sourceCitation: Harris Magical Papyrus (BM EA 10042) - Harris Magical Papyrus, recto col. 6/10, section K, 1-4 (Lange 1927: 53-54)

title: Fourteen Sherds from the Crossroad
intro: This lesson examines a fragmentary rite from the Maqlu Ritual Tablet involving fourteen potsherds gathered at a crossroads. Its accompanying declaration contrasts a witch with the speaker as a releaser, but the tablet breaks off before the sherds' destination is given.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet, preserved in 7th century BC manuscripts in Akkadian and Standard Babylonian, records a rite using fourteen sherds from a crossroad. The incantation includes the declaration, "My friend is a witch; but I am a releaser." The surviving passage ends with the words "to ..." before stating what should happen next.

In the rite's own terms, the sherds and the spoken declaration belong together. The language identifies the speaker as a releaser, while the collected fragments appear to serve as objects carried toward an intended but undocumented destination. The record preserves the materials and words, but not the completed sequence.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this fragment invites attention to how much meaning can rest on an unfinished instruction: the act of release is named, while its final movement is absent. The destination of the sherds, and therefore the rite's complete final action, remains uncertain. This entry is a historical reconstruction for study and reading, not a modern prescription.
reflection: How does the missing destination change your understanding of what the declaration, "I am a releaser," may have meant within this unfinished rite?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the surviving declaration aloud and journal what the fragment explicitly records versus what it leaves unknown. Do not attempt to reconstruct or perform the rite.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 70'

title: I Have Enclosed the Ford
intro: This lesson examines a protective boundary rite recorded in the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. The rite uses gypsum, roasted flour, and spoken words to enclose the space where a burning would take place.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records an exorcist drawing a closed circle around a vessel or crucible with gypsum and roasted flour. As the line is closed, the exorcist recites, "I have enclosed the ford." The passage appears in 7th century BC manuscripts of the Mesopotamian Akkadian or Standard Babylonian tradition, cited at obv. 21'-22'.

Within the rite's own terms, the circle marks a boundary around the working space. The words describe that boundary as a ford, or crossing place, and closing the line shuts it to anything hostile. The enclosure was made before the burning began, defining and protecting the area of action.

What is documented ends there. Read now, the rite can be considered as a focused act of defining limits before difficult work begins. Its materials and spoken phrase show how physical marking and language were joined in the protective logic of the ceremony. It remains uncertain how practitioners understood the hostile presence or how consistently this procedure was carried out beyond this record.
reflection: What kind of boundary helps you feel that a difficult task has a clearly defined beginning and end?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, arrange a few harmless objects in a visible circle around a journal or other everyday item. Read the phrase "I have enclosed the ford" aloud as a personal reminder to define a focused, protected space.
safetyNote: The historical account involves burning. Do not reproduce the burning; if using any flame for another purpose, follow basic fire safety and keep it away from people and combustible materials.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 21'-22'

title: I Trample Down My Foe
intro: This lesson examines a physical reversal rite recorded in the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. Its central action is the crushing of a dough figurine underfoot while reciting a short statement about overcoming a foe.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records placing a figurine made of dough on the ground and trampling it with the feet while reciting, "I trample down my foe." The source is cited at Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 86', within the Mesopotamian Akkadian or Standard Babylonian tradition. The surviving manuscripts date to the 7th century BC.

In its own terms, the rite made reversal physical rather than only verbal. The dough figurine represented the foe, and crushing it underfoot enacted the desired defeat through direct bodily action. The spoken phrase named that action as the practitioner performed it.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this rite can be studied as an example of how an image, a gesture, and a spoken line were joined to express opposition and reversal. The record does not explain who the foe was, how the figurine was made, or what results were expected beyond the stated action. It remains uncertain how this brief instruction fit into the larger performance of the ritual.
reflection: What does the shift from speaking about overcoming a foe to physically trampling a figurine reveal about the role of bodily action in this rite?
practice: As a modern study practice, read the recorded phrase aloud once and journal what the figurine and the act of trampling contribute beyond words alone. This is a reflective exercise, not a reconstruction of the historical rite.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 86'

title: O Nusku, These Are the Figurines of My Sorcerer
intro: This lesson examines a formal presentation in the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. Nine figurines are placed on a crucible while the sufferer identifies them to Nusku as images of the sorcerer and witch believed to have caused harm.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records nine figurines set in order on a crucible. The sufferer extends a finger toward them and recites a naming formula to Nusku, the fire and night-light god. The figurines are identified aloud as images of the sorcerer and witch before any fire touches them. This passage appears in 7th century BC manuscripts of the Mesopotamian Akkadian and Standard Babylonian tradition, at obv. 23'-26'.

Within the rite's own terms, naming and pointing establish the figurines as representations of the alleged harmful practitioners. The formal presentation brings the accusation before Nusku, while the crucible places the images in relation to the fire that will follow in the larger procedure. The sequence gives spoken identification a defined place before that next stage.

What is documented ends there in this entry. Read now, this scene can be considered a study in how accusation was given a physical and verbal form within a ritual sequence. It does not establish whether the accused person was known, present, or historically identifiable. The record does not explain beyond this passage how the naming formula was understood or what followed in detail.
reflection: What changes when an accusation is represented by figurines, pointed to, and spoken before a deity rather than left as an unspoken fear?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, arrange nine harmless objects in a row and write a short note describing what each object represents in a personal concern. Do not identify or target a real person, and do not use fire.
safetyNote: The historical procedure involves a crucible and fire. It is recorded for study and must not be attempted; the modern practice above uses no flame.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 23'-26'

title: Peeled Away Like Garlic
intro: This lesson examines a purification incantation from the second movement of the night in Maqlu. Its central image is the removal of spells layer by layer, like the skin of a garlic bulb.
body:
Maqlu, a Mesopotamian work in Akkadian and Standard Babylonian, records this line in Maqlu V, line 57. The incantation was recited while the household was fumigated and the patient's body was worked over by massage. The instruction continues as destructive rites give way to cleansing and protection.

Within the rite's own terms, harmful spells could be removed by treating them as layers that could be stripped away. The image of peeling garlic gives the purification a clear physical form: each layer is taken off until the unwanted influence is gone. Fumigation, massage, spoken words, cleansing, and protection appear together in this sequence.

Read now, this passage offers a focused image for release rather than a modern medical or magical prescription. You might understand the garlic image as a way to imagine burdens being removed gradually, without claiming that the historical rite worked in a modern sense. What remains uncertain is how the original practitioners understood the relationship between the fumigation, massage, spoken incantation, and final protection.
reflection: What burden would you choose to imagine being peeled away layer by layer, and what would cleansing and protection mean to you afterward?
practice: As a modern reflective practice, read the recorded phrase aloud once, then write down one concern you would like to set aside in layers. Do not recreate the historical fumigation or massage.
safetyNote: The historical account involves fumigation and massage. It is recorded here for study and should not be attempted as a reconstruction; avoid creating smoke or performing massage on another person as part of this practice.
sourceCitation: Maqlu V, line 57

title: Salt Charged at the Head of the Bed
intro: This lesson examines a short protective rite from the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. It centers on addressing salt, charging it through recitation, and placing it at the head of a sleeper's bed.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records a rite in which a lump of salt is addressed with the words, "You, O Salt, who were created in a pure place." The salt is then placed on a censer standing at the head of the bed. The source is cited as Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 113'-114', in 7th century BC manuscripts from the Mesopotamian Akkadian or Standard Babylonian tradition.

In the rite's own terms, the salt is treated as something that can be addressed and prepared through spoken words. Recitation charges the salt, while its position at the head of the bed places it beside the sleeper during the night. The recorded description connects the act with night protection, but it does not explain further how the protection was expected to operate.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this rite can be understood as a focused example of how speech, a material substance, and the sleeping space were joined in a protective setting. What remains uncertain is the precise meaning of the salt's creation in a pure place and the full ritual logic behind the censer. This entry is a historical reconstruction for study and reading, not a modern prescription.
reflection: What might the placement of charged salt at the head of the bed suggest about the relationship between spoken protection and the vulnerable state of sleep?
practice: As a modern study practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, read the recorded phrase aloud once and write a few sentences about how the words change your attention to the idea of nighttime protection. Do not treat the exercise as a historical or magical procedure.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 113'-114'

title: Seven Knots of White Wool
intro: This lesson examines a companion rite in the Maqlu Ritual Tablet that uses seven knots of white wool and an incantation about continuing sorcery. The rite concludes by undoing the knots and casting the wool band into a crucible.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records this rite in obv. 68'-69'. It belongs to the Mesopotamian Akkadian or Standard Babylonian tradition, preserved in 7th century BC manuscripts. The instructions describe tying seven knots in a band of white wool, reciting the words "They perform sorcery against me, they keep on performing sorcery against me," undoing the knots, and casting the band into the crucible. It is presented as a companion to a rite using three knots.

In its own terms, the procedure connects the knots with the continuing sorcery named in the incantation. Tying gives that condition a physical form, while undoing the knots represents its release. The final disposal of the band in the crucible completes the stated sequence. The record documents these actions, but it does not explain every symbolic meaning assigned to the number seven, the white wool, or the crucible.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this rite can be understood as a focused image of turning a repeated threat into something that can be loosened and set aside. What remains uncertain or debated is how ancient practitioners themselves understood the precise roles of the materials and number. Its value for study lies in observing how spoken words, counted knots, and removal were joined in one brief ritual pattern.
reflection: When a problem feels as though it keeps returning, what would it mean to give that repetition a form and then deliberately loosen it?
practice: As a modern reflective practice, write one recurring concern on paper and tie seven loose knots in a piece of thread while reading the sentence silently. Untie the knots one at a time as a symbolic act of release; this is not a reconstruction of the historical rite.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 68'-69'

title: Smearing the Door and Doorposts
intro: This lesson examines a sealing rite recorded in the Mesopotamian Maqlu Ritual Tablet. It centers on applying a mixture to a doorway while reciting the phrase "My hand is the Rainbow."
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records a rite in which the patient mixes roasted flour with a dry brewing substance in a porous clay flask or sherd. The patient then smears the mixture on the door, the bar, and the doorposts while reciting "My hand is the Rainbow." The surviving manuscripts are from the 7th century BC, and the passage is cited as Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 127'-129'.

In its own terms, this is a sealing action focused on the parts of the doorway that close, secure, and frame the entrance. The patient personally prepares the mixture and places it across the threshold structure, joining a physical substance with a spoken statement. The record presents the doorway treatment and the words together as one protective rite.

What is documented ends there. Read now, the rite can be considered an example of how a household boundary, a person's hand, and a named image were brought together in a protective gesture. It is uncertain what the Rainbow phrase specifically meant to the practitioners or how the mixture was understood beyond its use in the sealing action. This entry does not establish a modern effect for the rite.
reflection: What meaning might change when the patient, rather than another ritual specialist, personally prepares and applies the sealing substance at the doorway?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, write "My hand is the Rainbow" in a journal and note what your home's doorway represents as a boundary between outside activity and private space. Do not apply historical substances to the door or doorposts.
sourceCitation: Maqlu Ritual Tablet, obv. 127'-129'

title: The Clay Egg at the Prow
intro: This lesson examines a protective water spell from the Harris Magical Papyrus. The spell is spoken over an egg shaped from clay and given to the person standing at the front of a boat, with the stated aim of keeping crocodiles away from the vessel.
body:
The Harris Magical Papyrus records a spell spoken over an egg of clay. The entry belongs to the Ancient Egyptian tradition and dates to the 19th-20th Dynasty, around 1200-1100 BC. Its source citation identifies it as a spell spoken over a clay egg, with discussion in Forshaw thesis, p. 239.

In the recorded procedure, the spoken spell charges the clay object. The egg is then placed in the hand of the person at the prow, or front, of the boat. As the object travels ahead of the craft, it is understood to hold the river's animals away from the vessel.

What is documented ends there. Read now, this lesson shows how a spoken formula and a portable object were joined to a practical danger faced during travel. The record does not explain the words of the spell in this entry, and it remains uncertain how the rite was understood or carried out beyond these instructions. This is a historical reconstruction for study and reading, not a modern prescription.
reflection: What does the placement of the clay egg at the prow suggest about how protection was imagined to move through the space ahead of a traveling boat?
practice: As a modern practice rather than a reconstruction of the rite, write a brief intention for safe travel and read it aloud before placing the note with your travel belongings. Do not use it as a substitute for ordinary water safety.
safetyNote: The historical account involves crocodiles and travel by boat. Treat it as material for study, and do not approach crocodiles or attempt to test the procedure on the water.
sourceCitation: Harris Magical Papyrus (BM EA 10042) - Harris Magical Papyrus, spell spoken over an egg of clay (dd-tw r pn swHt n sin); Forshaw thesis, p. 239

title: The Clay Finger
intro: This lesson examines a small clay object recorded in the Maqlu Ritual Tablet. It belongs to a ritual context involving the spoken phrase "My murderess, my witch, and my sorceress" and the preparation of a finger-shaped model.
body:
The Maqlu Ritual Tablet records the making of a finger from clay. The object was rubbed with tallow and wrapped in red wool while the incantation "My murderess, my witch, and my sorceress" was recited. The entry also states that it was prepared exactly like the cornel sticks, without giving further details about those sticks here.

In the ritual's own terms, the shaped object, its coating, its red wrapping, and the spoken formula formed one connected act.
